doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: First hearing Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
summary: The Hot Fives were hard going with surface noise, but he felt their power; schoolmates found his tastes weird.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Can you recall what Louis Armstrong you first heard? Which part of his career?
Wow, that’s a good place to start.

Yeah, exactly. And I have to admit, when I first heard it I kind of didn’t know what to make of it because really the only stuff I was familiar with at that point, that being fifth grade you know, was Benny Goodman and Harry James and Count Basie, which I love that stuff. And to hear this at first I hadn’t heard anything that old at all of anything. And so the surface noise it was kind of a bad LP copy of it, it was a little bit of work to listen to but I knew it was hitting me hard. I mean I knew that this music was very powerful and great and that he was a great player of course. But it took me a while to really start getting into listening to music from that early on because I was sort of just, it was a little bit harder to listen to for me at that time because of the surface noise and all that.

Yeah. It’s hard to get past that kind of limited technology that they were using at the time, but it still sounds funny to hear you say that being in fifth grade I was only familiar with Benny Goodman, you know?

I know it kind of probably sounds funny. Not too many fifth graders these days or even when I was in fifth grade, were really interested in that. We were considered pretty weird by our classmates for being interested in it.
No, I was born in ‘64. So I guess ten years old is ‘74, ‘75.
